claims.text: The proposed target is a consolidated equimolar mixture of Pt, Pd, Ru, Rh, and Ir micropowders.
Ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation in liquid can be used to process the proposed five-noble-metal target.
Sufficiently rapid energy deposition suppresses the atomic mobility of noble-metal species during nucleation.
Suppressed atomic mobility during nucleation produces single-phase, chemically homogeneous Pt-Pd-Ru-Rh-Ir high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The ultrashort-pulse condition will produce nanoparticles with high or maximized surface-atom exposure.
A longer laser pulse permits greater atomic diffusion during nucleation.
The additional atomic diffusion enabled by a longer pulse promotes phase separation or elemental segregation.
Laser ablation in liquid forms a transient high-energy plume containing ablated atoms, ions, and clusters.
The plume cools, the ablated species condense, and condensate growth is ultimately quenched to release nanoparticles into the liquid.
Rapid plume cooling kinetically traps the constituent atoms in a random homogeneous solid-solution configuration.
Ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation has previously produced targeted equimolar five-element high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles from consolidated and heat-treated elemental micropowders.
The ultrashort-pulse condition will yield a single-phase homogeneous alloy, whereas the longer-pulse condition will show phase separation, segregation, or uncontrolled morphology.
The standard baseline laser-ablation pulse duration has previously yielded mixed outcomes.
The proposed mechanism applies when the constituent noble metals have comparable melting points and reduction kinetics.
The proposed mechanism may fail when constituent atomic diffusivities differ substantially.
The proposed mechanism may fail when nonuniform fluence or extreme plume instabilities dominate nanoparticle formation.
